claims.text: The target Mg-containing lightweight HEA has a density below 6 g/cm³.
The initial alloy is a uniform, metastable solid solution with Mg homogeneously dissolved in the matrix.
High-temperature exposure transforms the non-equilibrium solid solution into a phase-separated microstructure.
Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates form during the transformation.
Diffusion-controlled segregation of Mg out of a supersaturated solid solution drives phase separation and precipitation.
Mg-rich precipitates create local compositional variations in the matrix.
The local chemistry generated by phase separation promotes development of a continuous Mg-oxide scale during high-temperature oxidation.
The Mg-oxide scale is less protective than the oxide scale formed by the initial homogeneous state.
Formation of the less-protective oxide scale increases the oxidation rate.
Formation of the less-protective oxide scale diminishes corrosion resistance.
Aged alloys will have a larger volume fraction of Mg-rich intermetallics than the initial alloy.
Aging will coarsen the Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates.
The initial homogeneous alloy forms relatively protective and uniform oxide scales under comparable exposure conditions.
Variations in alloy composition and processing can alter the kinetics of phase transformation.

contradictions.description: The experiment is worded as applying 800–1050 °C thermal treatments both in air and in a 3.5 wt% NaCl solution. An aqueous NaCl solution cannot remain a solution at those temperatures under ordinary test conditions, so the high-temperature aging and aqueous-corrosion stages need to be specified as separate sequential exposures or assigned different conditions.
